slides.narration: Welcome to Book I, Chapter 19: Organizing Programs Across Multiple Files. This deck is built like the Chapter 1 lecture: the slide gives the conceptual claim, the workbench gives the code or evidence, and presenter notes tell you exactly what to say and do. The goal is not to rush through syntax. The goal is to make every claim accountable to an artifact: source text, compiler behavior, runtime output, an invariant, or a documented design boundary. Start by orienting learners to the chapter, then keep asking the same professional question: what would prove this explanation is true?

Recognition sounds like, 'I have seen this syntax.' Explanation sounds like, 'Here is the boundary, here is the rule, and here is the output or state that proves the rule held.' When you teach this, keep moving from vocabulary to mechanism to verification.

slides.title: 19.2.1 Understanding Separate Compilation
keyPoints: Each source file, after preprocessing its included material, forms a translation unit that the compiler checks.
A function used in one translation unit must have an appropriate declaration visible there.
The compiler does not automatically inspect every other source file in the directory to discover declarations.
Each source file, after preprocessing its included material, forms a translation unit that the compiler checks.
slides.narration: In this part of Chapter 19, use 19.2.1 Understanding Separate Compilation as an engineering claim, not a vocabulary word. Each source file, after preprocessing its included material, forms a translation unit that the compiler checks independently. A function used in one translation unit must have an appropriate declaration visible there. The compiler does not automatically inspect every other source file in the directory to discover declarations. Separate compilation supports incremental builds: changing one implementation may require recompiling only affected targets. Changing a widely included header can trigger much more work. This cost encourages stable, minimal interfaces, but do not sacrifice clarity merely to avoid every rebuild. Correct dependency tracking is more important than a fast build that accidentally reuses stale objects. The graduate-level move is to ask what evidence would make the claim trustworthy: a compiler diagnostic, a runtime value, a preserved invariant, or a boundary that failed cleanly. slides.title: 19.2.2 Understanding the Linker’s Role
keyPoints: The linker resolves references among compiled objects and libraries.
Every required noninline function definition must be supplied in a compatible form.
A missing source file in the link can cause an undefined reference even when all individual compilations succeeded.
The One Definition Rule constrains how entities are defined across the program.
slides.narration: In this part of Chapter 19, use 19.2.2 Understanding the Linker’s Role as an engineering claim, not a vocabulary word. The linker resolves references among compiled objects and libraries. Every required noninline function definition must be supplied in a compatible form. A missing source file in the link can cause an undefined reference even when all individual compilations succeeded. The One Definition Rule constrains how entities are defined across the program. Putting an ordinary noninline function definition in a header included by several source files can create multiple definitions. Inline functions and templates have different permitted patterns when their requirements are met. Do not resolve duplicate symbols by arbitrarily deleting object files; understand which entity was defined more than the language permits. The graduate-level move is to ask what evidence would make the claim trustworthy: a compiler diagnostic, a runtime value, a preserved invariant, or a boundary that failed cleanly. slides.title: 19.3.1 Using Include Guards
keyPoints: An include guard wraps a header in a unique macro condition so that its contents are not repeatedly processed.

Choose a project-specific guard name that is unlikely to collide with another header and avoid reserved identifier.
An include guard wraps a header in a unique macro condition so that its contents are not repeatedly processed.
slides.narration: In this part of Chapter 19, use 19.3.1 Using Include Guards as an engineering claim, not a vocabulary word. An include guard wraps a header in a unique macro condition so that its contents are not repeatedly processed within one translation unit. The pattern uses #ifndef, #define, and a matching #endif. Choose a project-specific guard name that is unlikely to collide with another header and avoid reserved identifier forms. A guard prevents repeated inclusion in one translation unit; it does not give an ordinary external definition permission to appear in multiple translation units. This distinction explains why a guarded header can still cause linker duplicate-definition errors. Header idempotence and program-wide definition rules solve different problems. slides.narration: In this part of Chapter 19, use Evidence and interpretation as an engineering claim, not a vocabulary word. slides.title: Header Declaration with Source-File Definition
keyPoints: Predict the output before running
Use stdout as behavioral evidence
Empty stderr matters because diagnostics have their own channel

slides.narration: This is a chapter listing, not a detached toy. Before running or reading it, state what behavior the program is supposed to witness. Header Declaration with Source-File Definition gives us an executable slice of Chapter 19. The expected stdout is not decorative; it is the behavioral witness for this example. The first visible line is '5'. If there are multiple lines, read them in order because order often encodes loop progression, branch selection, or state changes. Expected stderr is empty, which means normal behavior is being reported through stdout rather than the diagnostic channel. Expected exit code is 0, so the operating system sees the run as successful after the program finishes printing. If the displayed output ever differs after an edit, do not jump straight to 'wrong.' Ask which requirement changed, which path executed, and whether the difference belongs on stdout, stderr, or the process status.

question.prompt: What three things must you account for after the run?
question.answer: Account for stdout, stderr, and exit status. For this exercise, stdout should match the expected text, stderr should be empty, and exit status should be 0.

checks.prompt: Why is empty stderr worth saying out loud?
checks.answer: Because it proves normal results are not being smuggled through the diagnostic channel; many automated tests and scripts distinguish stdout from stderr.

checks.prompt: How should you explain exit code 0?
checks.answer: It is the process-level success signal. It does not replace checking stdout; it only says the program finished without reporting process failure.
